question:
Client: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi. Matter: motor accident claim, death of spouse.

Her husband was killed in a road accident involving a commercial truck. The truck driver was operating the vehicle without a valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies the claim, arguing the policy is void because the driver was unlicensed, and that it bears no liability.

Key facts: deceased aged 42; monthly income Rs 35,000; dependants are the wife and two minor children (8 and 12); the truck was a commercial vehicle owned by a transport company; the driver held no valid licence; the insurer contests liability.

Research the corpus and advise on supporting precedents, adverse precedents, and strategy.

Her husband was killed in a road accident involving a commercial truck. The truck driver was operating the vehicle without a valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies the claim, arguing the policy is void because the driver was unlicensed, and that it bears no liability.

Key facts: deceased aged 42; monthly income Rs 35,000; dependants are the wife and two minor children (8 and 12); the truck was a commercial vehicle owned by a transport company; the driver held no valid licence; the insurer contests liability.

args.question: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi's claim for motor accident compensation following death of her husband (aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, wife and two minor children dependants) caused by a commercial truck whose driver had no valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability arguing policy void due to unlicensed driver.

supporting.title: S. Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co. Ltd. & Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver lacked a specific endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle. The insurer's statutory duty to third parties overrides policy conditions.
supporting.fact_alignment: Like our case, this involved a commercial vehicle (Maxi Cab) where the insurer argued the driver lacked the proper licence/endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable to pay third-party compensation.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Supreme Court judgment that directly establishes that even where the driver's licence is deficient for a commercial vehicle, the insurer must still compensate the third-party victim. It anchors the 'pay first' principle.
supporting.quote: 'the insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained in the driving licence. In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer.'

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had only an LMV/transport endorsement but was driving a heavy goods vehicle — analogous to our case where the driver had no valid licence for a commercial truck. The court ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This High Court judgment applies Swaran Singh and S. Iyyapan to hold that even a clear licence deficiency (driving a class of vehicle not covered by the licence) does not exonerate the insurer vis-à-vis the third party. It confirms the pay-and-recover remedy.
supporting.quote: 'the mere fact that there was violation of the terms and conditions subject to which the insurance policy has been issued, cannot have the effect of exonerating the insurer from the statutory liability cast upon him in this regard to pay the amount to the third party victim.'

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: An insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver possessed only an LMV (non-transport) licence but was driving a goods vehicle (commercial). The court held the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner — directly on point.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Delhi High Court judgment comprehensively reviews the entire line of Supreme Court authority (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be avoided even on proof of conscious breach. It is a well-reasoned, authoritative statement of the law.
supporting.quote: 'even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor either in the same proceedings or by independent proceedings.'

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V. Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge required for a transport vehicle, the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and subsequently recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but no badge to drive a tourist maxi cab (commercial transport vehicle). The court ordered pay-and-recover — directly analogous to our commercial truck scenario.
supporting.why_it_matters: This confirms that even where the licence deficiency is clear and the insurer proves breach, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The third party is protected.
supporting.quote: 'Keeping in view the nature of injuries sustained by the claimant... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent - Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.'

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Even where the insurer proves a fundamental breach (driver with no licence), the insurer must pay the third-party claimant in the first instance under the 'pay and recover' principle, with liberty to recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all — the most extreme version of our facts. The tribunal still ordered pay-and-recover, citing Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba and Shamanna.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the closest factual match: a driver with absolutely no licence. Despite finding a 'fundamental and statutory breach,' the tribunal protected the third party by ordering pay-and-recover. It shows that even the strongest breach case does not defeat the third-party claim.
supporting.quote: 'the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time... it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1, owner of the offending vehicle.'

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: Even where the driving licence had lapsed and was not valid on the date of accident, the insurer must satisfy the third-party award and recover from the insured under the pay-and-recover principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired before the accident and was renewed only after — meaning no valid licence on the accident date. The court ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that even a clear licence invalidity (expired licence = no valid licence on accident date) does not defeat the third-party claim. The insurer pays first, then recovers.
supporting.quote: 'Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.'

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: The multiplier must be applied with reference to the age of the deceased; future prospects apply to self-employed individuals at standardized percentages; conventional heads are as per Pranay Sethi.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 42, self-employed — directly applicable to our facts for computing compensation.

supporting.quote: 'In case the deceased was self-employed or on a fixed salary, an addition of 25% where the deceased was between the age of 40 to 50 years should be regarded as the necessary method of computation.'

supporting.title: No.4 Is A Mother Of The Deceased Sri. M. ... vs No.1
supporting.principle: For deceased below 40 years with stable income, 50% future prospects must be added; for age 40-50, 30% addition applies.
supporting.fact_alignment: While the deceased here was 32 (below 40), the principle of adding future prospects for employed persons is established. For our deceased aged 42, the applicable addition is 25% (self-employed) or 30% (if permanent employment is shown).

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The Swaran Singh principle (insurer must pay third party despite licence defects) applies only to third-party claims, not own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that if the driver's licence was fake (not merely expired or wrong class), the breach is fundamental. However, the Supreme Court in this very case clarified at para 3 of the situations: 'In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.' So this case actually affirms pay-and-recover for third-party claims — it only limits Swaran Singh for own-damage claims. The risk is low because our case is a third-party death claim.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Laxmi Narain Dhut expressly holds that for third-party risks, the insurer must indemnify and recover. The ratio that Swaran Singh does not apply to own-damage claims is irrelevant here — this is a third-party death claim. The insurer cannot use this case to avoid liability; it actually supports pay-and-recover.
adverse.quote: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks... In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.'

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without any licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, and the insurer is not directly liable to indemnify the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that this case found the insurer 'absolved from its liability' because the driver had no licence. However, the tribunal still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third party. The risk is that the tribunal might first record a finding of fundamental breach — but the ultimate relief (pay-and-recover) remains intact for the claimant.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The tribunal in this very case ordered pay-and-recover despite finding a fundamental breach. The claimant still received full compensation from the insurer. The only risk is a delay if the insurer appeals the liability finding, but the third-party entitlement is not defeated.
adverse.quote: 'it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1, owner of the offending vehicle.'

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Driving without a licence can constitute contributory negligence reducing the claimant's compensation.
adverse.risk_to_client: This case is about the injured claimant himself driving without a licence (contributory negligence), not about the offending vehicle's driver being unlicensed. It is factually distinguishable and does not apply to our case where the deceased was a pedestrian/third party, not the driver.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The deceased in our case was not driving the vehicle — he was a third-party victim. Contributory negligence principles apply only when the deceased/claimant contributed to the accident. There is no allegation that the deceased contributed to the accident. This case is entirely distinguishable.

priority_arguments: 1. Statutory liability under Section 149 MV Act: The insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be avoided even if the driver lacked a valid licence. Cite S. Iyyapan (doc_032), Chennamma (doc_027), Satto (doc_033), and Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024).

2. Pay-and-recover: Even if the insurer proves breach, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The third-party claimant must not suffer due to the owner's fault. Cite all supporting precedents above.

3. Quantum: Deceased aged 42, self-employed, monthly income Rs 35,000. Apply multiplier of 14 (Sarla Verma), future prospects at 25% (Pranay Sethi for self-employed aged 40-50), deduct 1/3 for personal expenses (3 dependants), and claim conventional heads: loss of estate Rs 19,965, funeral Rs 19,965, spousal consortium Rs 40,000 + parental consortium Rs 40,000 each for two minor children (total Rs 1,59,720 as per Magma General and Satinder Kaur).

4. Burden of proof on insurer: The insurer must prove that the owner knowingly permitted an unlicensed driver to drive. Mere absence of a licence does not automatically prove conscious breach by the owner. The transport company owner may have been deceived by the driver.
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51 lakh to Rs 53 lakh) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of claim petition. The lower end assumes self-employed status (25% future prospects); the higher end if the deceased is shown to have been in permanent employment (30% future prospects).
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using the compute_quantum tool: Monthly income Rs 35,000 × 12 = Rs 4,20,000 annual. Add 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 42) = Rs 5,25,000. Deduct 1/3 for personal expenses (3 dependants) = Rs 3,50,000. Apply multiplier 14 (age 42) = Rs 49,00,000. Add conventional heads: loss of estate Rs 19,965 + funeral Rs 19,965 + consortium (spousal Rs 40,000 + two children at Rs 40,000 each = Rs 1,19,720) = Rs 1,59,650. Total: Rs 50,99,650.
risks: 1. The insurer may argue that a completely unlicensed driver (as opposed to one with a wrong-class or expired licence) constitutes a fundamental breach that should exonerate them entirely. However, Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) and the Supreme Court in Swaran Singh (cited throughout) reject this argument for third-party claims.

2. The insurer may argue that the transport company owner was negligent in hiring an unlicensed driver, and that this conscious breach should shift all liability to the owner. The response is that the third-party claim is against the insurer first; the insurer's recovery rights against the owner are a separate matter.

3. The insurer may dispute the income of Rs 35,000/month. Ensure documentary proof (salary slips, bank statements, IT returns, or employer certificate) is available. If the income is not fully documented, the tribunal may take a conservative notional income.
4. If the insurer proves that the owner knew the driver had no licence, the tribunal may still order pay-and-recover — the claimant is protected. No real risk to the claimant's entitlement.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim petition under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek a declaration that the insurer is liable to pay compensation with pay-and-recover rights against the owner. Also seek interest at 9% p.a. from the date of petition.

caveats: 1. The corpus does not contain a Supreme Court judgment directly on the point of a driver with absolutely NO licence (as opposed to expired or wrong-class licence) in a third-party death claim. However, Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) — a 2024 MACT decision — deals with exactly this scenario and orders pay-and-recover, and the Supreme Court in Swaran Singh (cited in multiple judgments) covers this situation.

2. The corpus contains no judgment that exonerates an insurer entirely from third-party liability on the ground that the driver had no licence. The consistent thread across all relevant judgments is that the insurer must pay the third party and may recover from the owner.

3. The quantum computation assumes the deceased was self-employed. If the deceased was in permanent employment, the future prospects addition would be 30% (not 25%), yielding a slightly higher figure. Counsel should ascertain the exact employment status.

4. The corpus does not contain judgments on the specific question of spousal and parental consortium for minor children in a death claim — the conventional heads are based on the Pranay Sethi framework as applied in doc_019 (Surendra Singh).

result.question: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi's claim for motor accident compensation following death of her husband (aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, wife and two minor children dependants) caused by a commercial truck whose driver had no valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability arguing policy void due to unlicensed driver.

supporting.title: S. Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co. Ltd. & Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver lacked a specific endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle. The insurer's statutory duty to third parties overrides policy conditions.
supporting.fact_alignment: Like our case, this involved a commercial vehicle (Maxi Cab) where the insurer argued the driver lacked the proper licence/endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable to pay third-party compensation.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Supreme Court judgment that directly establishes that even where the driver's licence is deficient for a commercial vehicle, the insurer must still compensate the third-party victim. It anchors the 'pay first' principle.
supporting.quote: 'the insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained in the driving licence. In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer.'

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had only an LMV/transport endorsement but was driving a heavy goods vehicle — analogous to our case where the driver had no valid licence for a commercial truck. The court ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This High Court judgment applies Swaran Singh and S. Iyyapan to hold that even a clear licence deficiency (driving a class of vehicle not covered by the licence) does not exonerate the insurer vis-à-vis the third party. It confirms the pay-and-recover remedy.
supporting.quote: 'the mere fact that there was violation of the terms and conditions subject to which the insurance policy has been issued, cannot have the effect of exonerating the insurer from the statutory liability cast upon him in this regard to pay the amount to the third party victim.'

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: An insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver possessed only an LMV (non-transport) licence but was driving a goods vehicle (commercial). The court held the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner — directly on point.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Delhi High Court judgment comprehensively reviews the entire line of Supreme Court authority (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be avoided even on proof of conscious breach. It is a well-reasoned, authoritative statement of the law.
supporting.quote: 'even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor either in the same proceedings or by independent proceedings.'

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V. Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge required for a transport vehicle, the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and subsequently recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but no badge to drive a tourist maxi cab (commercial transport vehicle). The court ordered pay-and-recover — directly analogous to our commercial truck scenario.
supporting.why_it_matters: This confirms that even where the licence deficiency is clear and the insurer proves breach, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The third party is protected.
supporting.quote: 'Keeping in view the nature of injuries sustained by the claimant... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent - Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.'

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Even where the insurer proves a fundamental breach (driver with no licence), the insurer must pay the third-party claimant in the first instance under the 'pay and recover' principle, with liberty to recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all — the most extreme version of our facts. The tribunal still ordered pay-and-recover, citing Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba and Shamanna.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the closest factual match: a driver with absolutely no licence. Despite finding a 'fundamental and statutory breach,' the tribunal protected the third party by ordering pay-and-recover. It shows that even the strongest breach case does not defeat the third-party claim.
supporting.quote: 'the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time... it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1, owner of the offending vehicle.'

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: Even where the driving licence had lapsed and was not valid on the date of accident, the insurer must satisfy the third-party award and recover from the insured under the pay-and-recover principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired before the accident and was renewed only after — meaning no valid licence on the accident date. The court ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that even a clear licence invalidity (expired licence = no valid licence on accident date) does not defeat the third-party claim. The insurer pays first, then recovers.
supporting.quote: 'Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.'
